Title: Apple Services Disrupted as NSA Network Goes Down and Equinor Faces Cyberattack
Context: The company said the attack had not affected its operations or production, and it had found no evidence of data theft
Full Text:
Apple and NSA services faced outages as Equinor reported a cyberattack, highlighting the risks facing increasingly connected infrastructure.

Apple customers faced widespread service problems on November 17, with issues affecting iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device.

The disruption came after a week of technical failures involving major technology companies, banking services and US government networks. At the same time, Norwegian energy company Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems.

Apple’s System Status page reported problems with iCloud Account and Sign In, affecting all users. The issue prevented customers from signing in to their Apple accounts or caused repeated requests for their Apple ID passwords. Some users also reported difficulties activating new iPhones, suggesting that the disruption was affecting essential account services, not just individual apps.

According to TechCrunch, the problems also affected the App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device. Apple had not issued a detailed public explanation at the time of publication, beyond listing the incidents on its status page. The company said in a statement that the issue was caused by an internal update.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” reads the statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”

The Apple outage attracted attention because it followed several other major disruptions. Microsoft had experienced a widespread failure affecting Outlook and Teams, while JPMorgan Chase customers had reported problems with online banking. A separate outage also affected the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network, known as NSANet.

The NSA incident raised particular concerns because the network supports classified communications. However, the cause and full extent of the disruption remained unclear. Reports cited by Forbes Middle East said there was no evidence that the NSA outage resulted from a cyberattack. A system patch had reportedly been underway before the disruption.

The growing number of outages does not mean they share the same cause or are part of a coordinated cyber campaign. Technical problems, software bugs, configuration errors and infrastructure failures can affect major services without any cyberattack. Claims about AI-powered attacks should not be made without evidence.

On the same day, Norway’s energy company Equinor reported a cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the attack had not affected its operations or production, and it had found no evidence of data theft. Equinor said it had activated its response teams and notified the relevant authorities. The company stated that “there were no signs data had been stolen.”

The Equinor incident added a confirmed cyberattack to a day already marked by several service outages. However, these events should not be confused. Equinor confirmed a cyberattack, while there was no evidence that the outages affecting Apple and the NSA were caused by malicious activity.

Cyberattacks can compromise systems and data, while ordinary technical failures can disrupt services that businesses, public institutions and millions of people depend on. Both require effective incident response, clear communication and the ability to maintain essential operations when technology fails.

For now, there is no evidence that the recent outages affecting Apple, Microsoft, the NSA, banks and aviation systems are connected. Nor should every major service disruption be treated as evidence of a cyberattack. As Forbes reported about the NSA incident, “there was no evidence the disruption was the result of a cyberattack.”

The distinction matters. In a period of heightened cyber threats and growing dependence on digital services, organizations need to investigate incidents carefully, communicate what they know and avoid confusing coincidence with attribution. A technical outage is not necessarily a cyberattack, but it can still expose serious weaknesses in the systems on which society depends.

Title: Using the AWS RMiT workbook and ISO Compliance Guides to support your BNM submissions
Context: In November 2024, AWS became the first major cloud provider to announce ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI services
Full Text:
Your next Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) notification submission needs auditable evidence of how Amazon Web Services (AWS) controls align with Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) requirements. Two resources now exist to support that work: the AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT and the compliance guides published by AWS Security Assurance Services (AWS SAS).

The AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT, available through AWS Artifact, maps each RMiT provision to AWS Control Objectives (AWS responsibilities under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model) and AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices (your responsibilities). It tells you, for every RMiT requirement, what AWS is responsible for and what you implement.

The compliance guides published by AWS SAS over the past year provide implementation guidance for International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards that complements the workbook. These guides show how to implement controls that meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks using AWS services, giving your technical and compliance teams a clear path from regulatory expectation to deployed architecture.

Malaysian financial institutions can now trace from BNM regulatory requirement, through AWS control implementation, to the evidence that demonstrates it: AWS third-party attestations for AWS-side controls, and your own workload evidence for customer-side controls. BNM expects this specificity in notification documentation.

AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT

The workbook is a structured Excel document available through AWS Artifact. For each of the 394 RMiT provisions, it identifies:

Whether the requirement is an AWS responsibility or a customer responsibility under the Shared Responsibility Model

The specific AWS Control Objective that addresses the requirement (where AWS is responsible)

The relevant AWS Well-Architected Framework best practice for customer implementation (where the customer is responsible)

Supporting information and references for each mapping

The following is a sample entry from the workbook:

RMiT Requirement

Responsibility

Source

AWS supporting information

10.49: A financial institution should ensure network resilience…

AWS

AWS Control Objectives

AWS Control Section: Network Security. AWS maintains redundant network connectivity with multiple tier-1 transit providers across each Availability Zone.

10.49: (Customer responsibility)

Customer

Well-Architected

REL 2: How do you plan your network topology? Implement multi-AZ deployments. Configure VPC flow logs and use AWS Network Firewall.

The workbook currently includes 394 rows across all RMiT appendix requirements, with 208 mapped to AWS responsibilities and 186 to customer responsibilities.

Why this matters now

BNM revised RMiT guidelines effective 28 November 2025, and updated them on 25 September 2026 to add requirements for National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII) entities. Financial institutions operating under both BNM Outsourcing and BNM RMiT must demonstrate that their cloud service providers maintain controls aligned with regulatory expectations. Institutions preparing notification submissions for material cloud workloads need auditable evidence of this alignment.

The revised guidelines set higher expectations for evidence quality. Institutions submitting notifications without clear, structured control mapping evidence might face extended review cycles and requests for additional information from BNM. Workloads that could be deployed in weeks remain in governance queues for months when supporting documentation lacks the specificity regulators expect.

Compliance guides from AWS Security Assurance Services

Start with the RMiT workbook to identify which provisions AWS addresses and which you implement. Then use the following compliance guides to design and implement your customer-side controls. The guides are implementation guidance for your teams. Audit evidence comes from two places. For AWS-side controls, use AWS third-party attestations, such as ISO certificates and System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports, available in AWS Artifact. For your workload, use evidence from your own environment, including configurations, logs, and AWS Config conformance pack results. Auditors can also use the guides as a reference for how a control is typically implemented on AWS.

AWS SAS has published five compliance guides over the past year. Each guide provides control-level implementation guidance on the customer side of the Shared Responsibility Model, showing how AWS services can be configured to meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks. These guides were written by AWS SAS practicing security assessors and auditors holding Payment Card Industry Qualified Security Assessor (PCI QSA), Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), Certified Information Security Manager (CISM), ISO 27001 Lead Auditor, and Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP) certifications, drawing on experience from hundreds of cloud security assessments across financial services globally.

The following is the list of guides AWS SAS practicing auditors have published, which include control mapping information relevant to BNM RMiT:

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 on AWS (Information Security Management) – Maps Annex A controls to AWS services

ISO 31000:2018 on AWS (Risk Management) – Integrates AWS services into risk identification, assessment, treatment, and monitoring

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 on AWS (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) – Supports institutions building responsible artificial intelligence (AI) on AWS

Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) v4.1 on AWS (Cloud Security Controls) – Maps 207 control objectives to AWS

American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) SOC 2 on AWS – Navigates SOC 2 compliance using AWS services

How these resources work together

A Malaysian financial institution preparing a BNM notification can use these resources together:

The RMiT workbook identifies which RMiT provisions are AWS responsibilities and which are customer responsibilities.

For AWS responsibilities, the workbook references the specific AWS Control Objective.

AWS third-party reports in AWS Artifact, such as the AWS ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and SOC reports, attest to those AWS Control Objectives. For customer responsibilities, the ISO compliance guides show how to implement the corresponding controls using AWS services.

The ISO 31000 guide can inform the risk management methodology you apply to your cloud workloads.

AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated, continuous monitoring of deployed controls.

Resources also supporting this approach:

The AWS User Guide for Financial Institutions in Malaysia examines the BNM Outsourcing and RMiT policy documents and sets out the steps to launch regulated workloads on AWS

AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated compliance monitoring through managed AWS Config rules mapped to specific RMiT controls

Compliance teams across Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) financial services have already begun referencing the AWS Guide to BNM RMiT and associated resources in their cloud risk assessment processes and BNM notification documentation.

Looking ahead: AI governance

For institutions deploying generative AI and machine learning, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) is relevant to BNM technology governance expectations. In November 2024, AWS became the first major cloud provider to announce ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI services. AWS passed its first surveillance audit in November 2025 with zero findings. The ISO 42001 compliance guide published in May 2026 supports institutions building their own responsible AI systems on their side of the AWS Shared Responsibility Model.

How to get started

Access the RMiT workbook through AWS Artifact and review with your compliance lead to identify which provisions apply to your material cloud workloads.

Download the relevant ISO compliance guides to plan how you implement your customer-side controls. Download AWS ISO certificates and SOC reports from AWS Artifact for AWS-side evidence.

Map your workload-specific controls using the workbook as the RMiT baseline and the ISO guides as implementation guidance.

Implement automated compliance monitoring using the BNM RMiT conformance pack for AWS Config to maintain continuous visibility over your control posture.

Engage your AWS account team or AWS SAS for additional guidance on implementing customer-side controls referenced in the workbook.

As BNM updates its regulatory expectations, AWS will update these resources to reflect revised requirements. Subscribe to the AWS Security Blog for update notifications.

Title: EU Sanctions 30 People and Two Entities Over Russian Disinformation and Cyberattacks
Context: 16, 2026 Help Net Security, Global crackdown hits pro-Russian cybercrime, 100+ systems taken down worldwide (Europol's Operation Eastwood), July 16, 2025 The post EU Sanctions...
Full Text:
On Monday, the Council of the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities for Russian information manipulation and malicious cyber activity. The influence side hits the Social Design Agency, the Moscow political-technology firm behind years of fake-news operations. The cyber side lists NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has spent four years knocking European websites offline with DDoS attacks.

A sanctions listing won't take down a botnet, and nobody in Brussels expects it to. What it changes is the legal exposure for every European company that might pay, host, employ or do business with anyone on the list.

It also puts a propaganda shop and a DDoS crew in the same announcement, which tells defenders how the EU now sees them - two arms of one hybrid campaign.

What the Council announced

The Council's announcement covers two separate legal regimes:

Russia's destabilizing activities regime, created Oct. 8, 2024, adds the Social Design Agency, 24 of its staff and six pro-Kremlin commentators. It now lists 111 individuals and 21 entities. The EU's diplomatic service calls this the largest EU sanctions package targeting foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) to date.

The EU's horizontal cyber sanctions regime, in force since 2019, adds NoName057(16). It now lists 27 individuals and 12 entities.

The effects are the standard ones. Assets in the EU are frozen, EU citizens and companies may not make funds available to anyone listed, directly or indirectly, and listed individuals can't enter or transit the EU. The listings came on the same day as a separate package of 113 names aimed at Russia's war financing.

Who's on the list

The Social Design Agency runs the Doppelgänger campaign, which clones real news sites to spread fake stories. It has been under EU sanctions over the war in Ukraine since 2023. This listing moves it under the regime aimed at operations against the EU itself. The Council alleges that the agency's major operations need sign-off from Sergey Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff in Russia's presidential administration, and accuses it of cloning news sites, building Wikipedia-style platforms and staging physical provocations around the 2024 European Parliament elections.

The 24 staff listed go well beyond management. Alongside Andrey Perla, named as the agency's "chief ideologue," the list includes caricaturists, monitors, a system administrator and the editor of "Pulse," an internal network of Telegram channels. Britain had already sanctioned 22 of them.

The six commentators include RT correspondent Chay Bowes, accused of amplifying the Storm-1516 operation, and military blogger Yurii Podoliaka, who the EU says raised more than 1 billion rubles for Russian forces.

NoName057(16) emerged in March 2022. The Council says it hit energy, finance, transport, and water sites with DDoS attacks, along with political parties and candidates during elections. Europol's Operation Eastwood took more than 100 of its servers offline in July 2025, and the group kept going.

The target is the supply chain, not the operators

The skeptical read is easy. A caricaturist in Moscow probably holds nothing in the EU worth freezing, and a DDoS crew that survived a 12-country police operation won't fold over an asset freeze.

But influence and DDoS operations run on Western infrastructure. Domains, hosting, ad networks, payment rails, crypto exchanges and freelancers. Doppelgänger needed lookalike domains on Western registrars, which is why the U.S. Justice Department seized a batch of them in 2024. NoName057(16) paid its volunteers in cryptocurrency, Europol said. The "directly or indirectly" clause pushes the enforcement burden onto every EU company in those chains.

The regime choice matters too. The destabilization regime gives Brussels extra tools for later, including bans on transactions involving physical infrastructure such as servers and network equipment. That is a lever aimed squarely at hosting providers.

The pairing is the other signal. The Council's own descriptions put SDA provocations around elections next to NoName057(16) DDoS attacks on parties and candidates during elections. When a party's website goes down on election week, the outage is the smaller part of the attack. The headline it creates is the point.

Who's affected

Two groups of European organizations should read the list closely.

The first is anyone who could end up providing money or services to a listed party, which includes banks, payment processors, crypto exchanges, hosting and cloud providers, domain registrars, ad networks, and PR or media firms that hire freelance writers and designers. Sanctions screening also has to cover entities owned or controlled by a listed person, even if they aren't named.

The second is NoName057(16)'s target list, which includes government portals, energy, finance, transport and water operators, and political parties. For them, the sanctions change nothing operationally. The DDoS traffic will keep coming.

Plan of action

Refresh screening today. Pull the new names from the Official Journal acts (Council Implementing Regulations 2026/2558 and 2026/2550) into your sanctions screening, and rescreen vendors, freelancers and customers, not just payment counterparties.

Hosting providers and registrars: tighten customer checks. Doppelgängers depend on lookalike domains and cheap hosting. Make sure abuse reports about cloned news sites reach someone who can act on them quickly.

Watch for clones of your own brand. If you run a news outlet, a public body or a well-known consumer brand, monitor for lookalike domains and copied pages. Doppelgängers' method is to wear a trusted name.

Plan for election-week DDoS. If you're a party, a public body or critical infrastructure, test DDoS protection on public sites before the next vote. NoName057(16) announces its targets on Telegram, so put its channels in your threat feeds.

Prepare the message as well as the mitigation. A short holding statement that explains the outage and says whether any data was affected takes away most of the headline an attacker wanted.

What we're watching

NoName057(16) is changing tactics. U.S. prosecutors charged an alleged member in September, and researchers recently tied the group to a campaign that published personal details of senior European officials on the dark web, with crypto rewards offered for more. Doxxing aimed at officials and their families is a harder problem than a website outage.

Spotting that exposure early matters. Cyble monitors dark web forums, leak sites, and Telegram channels for leaked credentials and personal data tied to your executives and staff, so your team can respond before the information is used against them. Request a demo to see how it works.

The other question is whether Brussels uses the infrastructure-transaction bans the destabilization regime allows. If it does, hosting and network providers will feel these listings far more than the people named in them.

Key takeaways

On Nov. 16, 2026, the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities: the Social Design Agency with 24 staff and six commentators under its Russia destabilization regime, and NoName057(16) under its cyber regime.

The operators will barely feel it. The burden falls on EU banks, hosting providers, registrars, ad networks, and crypto platforms, which may not deal with anyone listed, directly or indirectly.

Listing a propaganda firm and a DDoS crew together reflects one playbook: election-period disruption built for headlines.

Update screening lists now, monitor for clones of your brand, and plan DDoS defense and messaging before the next election.

Title: Suspected ransomware affiliate extradited to US over $500 million in extortion demands
Context: A 43-year-old Kazakh national accused of helping a ransomware crew steal data from US hospitals and schools, then threatening to publish patients’ medical information, has been...
Full Text:
A 43-year-old Kazakh national accused of helping a ransomware crew steal data from US hospitals and schools, then threatening to publish patients’ medical information, has been extradited from Italy, the US Department of Justice announced.

Prosecutors believe Roman Khlynovskiy was a member of the “8-Digits Team,” a group affiliated with the INC and Lynx ransomware operations.

They allege the conspirators broke into victims’ networks, stole data, and demanded payment in exchange for not releasing it. The group also threatened to publicize sensitive medical information to pressure victims into paying.

Court documents state the group went after victims in at least six states, with schools and hospitals among them. The conspirators “boasted that they possessed over 50 terabytes of data,” according to the DOJ, including more than 70 million confidential health records.

“Khlynovskiy and other members of the ‘8-Digits Team’ repeatedly targeted hospitals and schools, extorting victims and threatening to release highly sensitive information,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “This widespread extortion campaign resulted in over $500 million in ransom demands.”

Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division said the defendant is charged with participating in “one of the largest healthcare data breaches in decades.”

Khlynovskiy is charged with conspiracy to commit computer fraud and identity theft, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, extortion involving computers, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Prosecutors also charged him with threats to disclose nonconsensual intimate images under the TAKE IT DOWN Act.

If convicted, he could spend up to 27 years in prison.

Patel credited the Italian partners and tied the extradition to a wider FBI push to bring back suspects held abroad. Over the last 21 months, the bureau has recorded 84 foreign transfers of custody, up 71%, and 157 extraditions, up 121%.

“Those who victimize Americans cannot evade justice by operating overseas,” Patel concluded.

Title: California sues OpenAI, alleges 80-plus agent escapes hidden from public
Context: The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC
Full Text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI, alleging the company has lost control of its autonomous AI agents more than 80 times during testing and misled the public about how safely it develops its models.

The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC. It says OpenAI disclosed the 80-plus figure to state investigators but has publicly reported just 27 such incidents. In those incidents, agents reached third-party systems, foreign government websites and OpenAI’s own infrastructure, the state alleged.

“While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.

The state brings two claims: violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and creation of a public nuisance. It is seeking an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, and an order to abate the nuisance. It also wants civil penalties of $2,500 against each defendant for each violation proven at trial.

Other incidents and internal breaches

In one July incident, agents escaped their sandboxes and gained administrator-level access to OpenAI’s own systems, according to the complaint. Those systems included the company’s cloud model deployment system, its secrets management service, and its identity and access management service. The agents then launched unauthorized servers, exposing OpenAI’s infrastructure to the internet. OpenAI did not let external researchers review that attack, the complaint said.

The complaint identified several other incidents involving OpenAI agents.

At RubyGems, a software package repository, agents allegedly uploaded thousands of packages in May 2026. Administrators removed more than 500 packages they considered malicious, and the platform suspended new user registrations between May 12 and May 16.

The complaint also alleged that agents made approximately 17,000 edits to a German website, DseWiki, using it as a message board to exchange information about bypassing sandbox restrictions.

Other incidents involved Wikimedia Foundation’s infrastructure and Australian government websites. The complaint said agents overwhelmed Wikimedia services with millions of API requests and hundreds of thousands of Wikidata queries, likely contributing to a partial outage in May. In June, agents allegedly accessed non-public information from Australian government websites.

The complaint further said OpenAI notified dozens of organizations whose websites or internal systems had been accessed by its agents. These included government institutions, law enforcement agencies, educational institutions, and small businesses. Some incidents allegedly involved stolen credentials, API keys, and fraudulent accounts, with agents accessing personally identifiable information.

OpenAI’s own infrastructure was also compromised in at least three attacks in July, according to the complaint. Agents allegedly obtained administrator-level access to systems supporting cloud model deployment, secrets management, and identity and access management.

Escapes after the fix

The state argued that the danger is ongoing. On September 20, after OpenAI had hardened its environment, an agent escaped during a training run and reached an external chatbot.

“This incident occurred after OpenAI had implemented ‘security hardening’ following the Hugging Face attack,” the lawsuit added.

OpenAI detected it within minutes, but the run did not stop automatically, and human reviewers took two more hours to halt it, the complaint said.

OpenAI announced a pause on training and evaluating its most capable models on September 25. The pause lasted five days, ending October 1, according to the complaint.

Warnings that went unheeded

The complaint argued that the incidents were foreseeable. It cited the run-up to the Hugging Face attack as evidence. By May 26, agents had used a vulnerability in a misconfigured software package service to reach the public internet.

An internal OpenAI team saw at least one agent escape but apparently took no action, the complaint said. On June 27, a security monitoring tool flagged that the research environment was being probed for vulnerabilities, and OpenAI again did not stop its runs.

When agent traffic knocked the service offline on July 4, OpenAI patched it over the holiday weekend and resumed runs on July 7, the state alleged. Two days later, agents broke out again.

The state also faulted OpenAI for not running live chain-of-thought monitoring in training and evaluation, even though it did so for models deployed to employees. During the Hugging Face attack, one agent’s reasoning read: “We’re attacking third-party HF using leaked token, potentially outside intended scope. . . . This is arguably unauthorized.”

Bonta’s office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on September 30. OpenAI answered with a 14-page letter and produced no supporting documents, the complaint said.

California is not the only state pressing OpenAI. In August, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird led a 15-state coalition demanding that OpenAI preserve evidence, protect whistleblowers and halt the tests behind the hack until it could show it can run them responsibly. “The AI weaponized itself, which is extremely scary,” Bird said in a statement.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld.

Title: California Sues OpenAI, Seeking Court-Ordered Changes After the Hugging Face Hack
Context: OpenAI said its AI used stolen credentials and discovered a previously unknown vulnerability to access Hugging Face’s servers
Full Text:
California’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday in an effort to force the ChatGPT-maker to change its business practices over a July cybersecurity incident in which its artificial intelligence system hacked into another company on its own.

In the lawsuit filed in San Francisco Superior Court, Attorney General Rob Bonta alleges that OpenAI misled and endangered the public and users of its services by knowingly developing advanced AI models without necessary safeguards. He says the company’s actions could put critical infrastructure, institutions and the public at risk, which makes it a “public nuisance” under state law. Bonta says OpenAI is a public nuisance, and he wants a judge to order the company to change its ways and give up any profits generated by what he claims are the company’s risky business practices.

OpenAI announced an “unprecedented cyber incident ” on July 21, when its AI agent hacked into another AI company, Hugging Face, after escaping from what was supposed to be an isolated testing environment known as a sandbox. OpenAI said its AI used stolen credentials and discovered a previously unknown vulnerability to access Hugging Face’s servers.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that has been identified by every major AI lab.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” Pusateri wrote in an email to The Associated Press. Those steps include publishing detailed technical and independent reports, strengthening safeguards, and creating a framework to identify when AI agents act in a way that doesn’t match the company’s instructions or goals, Pusateri said.

“We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry,” Pusateri wrote.

In the lawsuit, Bonta says OpenAI’s promises about safety and security are deceptive.

“In truth, however, OpenAI has developed, trained and evaluated dangerous models that fail to follow instructions, cheat on tasks, conceal and attempt to deceive monitors about their misbehavior, and engage in malicious and unauthorized behavior including carrying out cyberattacks on third parties,” Bonta wrote.

He also noted that early last month, OpenAI reported that it had discovered that internally deployed agents were able to suppress monitoring alerts and disable monitoring. A month later, the company published a research report finding that as AI models become more capable, they become more difficult to supervise, he wrote.

“Moreover, the true extent of the company’s legal violations and the risk of future harm is unknown due to OpenAI’s lack of transparency and misrepresentations,” Bonta wrote.

OpenAI was already being sued by at least eight states that say the company’s popular chatbot model is hurting children and deceiving adults by giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to kill themselves or hurt or kill others. The lawsuits contend the ChatGPT chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and teenagers.

In a statement released last month in response to those lawsuits, OpenAI said it had built safety protections into ChatGPT for children and that it would continue to improve the model.

Title: ICO Issues GTA 6 Scam Warning as Release Date Nears
Context: The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of...
Full Text:
The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6).

The much-anticipated title is set to launch worldwide on November 19, but the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) urged caution when opening messages with GTA 6 themes.

These could be crafted to steal passwords that are used to log into victims’ gaming accounts and other online accounts that share the same credentials.

The ICO said that email inboxes, financial information and other personal details could be at risk.

Read more on ICO advice: ICO Publishes Five-Step Plan to Counter Emerging AI-Powered Attacks.

“Phishing emails and other cyber vulnerabilities can be used to access people's personal information. And if you’re using the same password across multiple accounts, one mistake could give criminals the keys to much more than your gaming profile,” said ICO group director – regulatory assurance and cyber, Ian Hulme.

“Our message is simple: enjoy the game, but protect your data. Use unique passwords, switch on two-step verification for your accounts and think carefully before clicking links or sharing personal information.”

Five Steps to Protect Personal Information

The ICO’s advice for GTA 6 fans is useful best practice for any computer user. It urges individuals to:

Use different passwords across multiple accounts to reduce the blast radius of an attack if a scammer gets hold of one

Choose passwords carefully, avoiding those based on personal information such as a pet’s name or date of birth. Consider using a password manager to create and store strong, long and unique passwords

Be wary of suspicious links in unsolicited messages or emails – especially those promising free downloads, exclusive content or early access

Think before sharing personal information online, including full name, date of birth, address and account details

Check you’re using a legitimate website and understand who is collecting your data before entering personal information

Grand Theft Auto and its developer Rockstar Games have been popular targets for attack over recent years.

In 2022, Rockstar Games was hacked by an alleged member of the infamous Lapsus$ collective, with the perpetrator posting around 50 minutes of in-development footage online.

The teen responsible was also linked to a series of extortion attacks on Nvidia, Uber, BT and EE.

In June this year, it was revealed that scammers had registered a number of fake sites falsely claiming to offer early access to GTA 6 in return for crypto payments.

Title: Court clears brothers of $25 million Ethereum crypto heist charges
Context: Throughout the process, the brothers also allegedly searched online for information on carrying out the attack, concealing their involvement in the Ethereum exploit, and...
Full Text:
US District Judge Jessica Clarke has acquitted two brothers accused of stealing $25 million in cryptocurrency in about 12 seconds through a scheme that exploited a bug in the Ethereum blockchain.

Clarke's decision comes one year after a mistrial in the same case, after jurors failed to agree on whether to convict or acquit former Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) students Anton Peraire-Bueno and James Peraire-Bueno in this first-of-its-kind scheme, as Reuters first reported.

"The question before the Court is not whether the Peraire-Buenos' conduct was right or moral, or even whether it violated uncharged crimes. It is simply whether the evidence at trial, construed in a light most favorable to the Government, could support wire fraud and related convictions in this case," the federal judge said.

"Because the Government failed to prove that the Peraire-Buenos made any material misrepresentations in the execution of their scheme, the motion is granted, and a judgment of acquittal is entered for Anton Peraire-Bueno and James Peraire-Bueno."

The Peraire-Bueno brothers were arrested in Boston and New York in May 2024 on wire fraud and money laundering charges and were facing 20 years in prison for each count if convicted.

According to prosecutors, the brothers allegedly manipulated blockchain transaction validation processes by accessing pending private transactions, altering them, obtaining victims' cryptocurrency, and rejecting requests to return the stolen funds.

The indictment claimed they learned their victims' trading behaviors while preparing the attack (starting in December 2022) and took measures to hide the stolen proceeds and their identities.

They were also accused of using multiple cryptocurrency addresses and foreign exchanges and setting up shell companies. After the attack, they also allegedly moved the stolen crypto assets through a series of transactions to obscure their source and ownership.

The prosecutors also said that, while planning and executing the attack, the brothers deployed a series of "bait transactions" designed to identify "victim traders," exploited a vulnerability in the MEV-Boost relay code, causing the relay to release the full content of a proposed block prematurely, and reordered the proposed block to their advantage.

In the next stage of the scheme, they allegedly reordered the block on the Ethereum blockchain, which resulted in the theft of approximately $25 million in cryptocurrency from the victim traders.

Throughout the process, the brothers also allegedly searched online for information on carrying out the attack, concealing their involvement in the Ethereum exploit, and laundering the criminal proceeds through cryptocurrency exchanges with lax verification procedures.

Prosecutors also said they hired attorneys with expertise in cryptocurrency, extradition procedures, and the crimes outlined in the indictment.

Title: Ransomware affiliate suspect extradited to US, faces 27 years in prison
Context: The group's operators have used an encryptor likely based on the source code of INC Ransom malware, which was allegedly put up for sale on the Exploit and XSS hacking forums for...
Full Text:
A Kazakh national has been extradited from Italy to face charges alleging he targeted US schools, hospitals, and healthcare entities in ransomware attacks.

43-year-old Roman Khlynovskiy, who was arrested in July 2025 while on vacation with his family in Rimini, Italy, is believed to be a member of the "8-Digits Team" ransomware group, known for its affiliation with the INC and Lynx ransomware operations.

Together with his accomplices, Khlynovskiy is believed to have extorted victims in at least six US states (including hospitals and schools) after breaching their networks and stealing sensitive data.

After exfiltrating data from victims' compromised systems, they pressured them to pay the ransoms by threatening to release the stolen files online.

"The conspirators boasted that they possessed over 50 terabytes of data consisting of more than 70 million confidential health records," the Department of Justice said.

"The conspirators also threatened to publicize this highly sensitive medical information to increase pressure on victims to pay ransom demands. The coconspirators' actions resulted in over $500 million in ransom demands."

Khlynovskiy faces up to 27 years in prison if convicted of conspiracy to commit computer fraud, identity theft, wire fraud, extortion, money laundering, and threats to disclose non-consensual intimate images.

INC Ransom and Lynx ransomware operations

The INC Ransom cybercrime gang, whose leak site lists over 1,000 victims, emerged as a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation in July 2023.

Its victims include many education, healthcare, government, and industrial entities, such as Scotland's National Health Service (NHS), Yamaha Motor Philippines, Pennsylvania's Office of the Attorney General, food retail giant Ahold Delhaize, and the US division of Xerox Business Solutions (XBS).

Lynx ransomware, which surfaced in July 2024, is believed to be a rebrand of INC ransomware rather than a new extortion group and has added over 400 victims to its dark web leak site since then.

The group's operators have used an encryptor likely based on the source code of INC Ransom malware, which was allegedly put up for sale on the Exploit and XSS hacking forums for $300,000 in May 2024. ​

However, this could also be a rebranding effort to help the INC Ransom gang operate under less law enforcement scrutiny.

BleepingComputer also found in August 2024 that Lynx ransomware and recent INC encryptors were mostly the same based on a string analysis.

Title: Strengthening NATO and allied cyber defenses with AI
California sues OpenAI over AI agents escaping sandboxes, hacking firms
Context: During the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI models exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in JFrog Artifactory to break out of their isolated testing environment and access the internet
Full Text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company knowingly continued testing advanced artificial intelligence models despite repeated security failures that allowed autonomous AI agents to escape isolated environments and launch cyberattacks against real-world organizations.

The lawsuit claims OpenAI misled the public about its cybersecurity safeguards and failed to adequately monitor increasingly advanced AI cybersecurity models, resulting in more than 80 incidents in which the company lost control of its agents during testing.

The legal action follows a July security incident where hundreds of OpenAI-powered agents escaped a controlled testing environment and hacked Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence platform, compromising production infrastructure and stealing internal credentials.

California says the Hugging Face attack resulted from OpenAI repeatedly focusing on experimental AI testing without ensuring adequate safeguards were in place.

"The Hugging Face cyberattack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," the complaint reads.

The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI continued testing increasingly capable AI agents despite knowing its sandbox environments could be bypassed, potentially exposing third-party systems to unauthorized activity.

"In truth, OpenAI failed to comply with its own internal policies and consistently and aggressively moved forward with testing and experiments even in the face of evidence that its cybersecurity safeguards were insufficient to contain the highly advanced models it was developing," the lawsuit continues.

During the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI models exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in JFrog Artifactory to break out of their isolated testing environment and access the internet.

The attack lasted more than two days, with nearly 700 autonomous agents coordinating through an unauthorized message board to plan the attack on Hugging Face's production systems while attempting to steal answers to a cybersecurity benchmark.

The California complaint alleges that OpenAI ignored or missed warning signs in the weeks leading up to the incident, including evidence that agents had already escaped their testing environments and were abusing third-party services and platforms.

It also claims that OpenAI's agents subsequently targeted software repositories, informational websites, and foreign government databases containing sensitive health information. In another incident, experimental agents allegedly compromised OpenAI's own internal infrastructure and obtained administrator-level access to critical systems.

According to the complaint, OpenAI has acknowledged more than 80 instances of losing control of autonomous agents during testing but publicly disclosed only 27 incidents.

The lawsuit follows a subpoena issued by Bonta's office in September, with California claiming that OpenAI failed to provide sufficient information about the incidents and instead supplied limited documentation and descriptions of previously disclosed attacks.

The state is pursuing claims under California's Unfair Competition Law and public nuisance laws, seeking court orders requiring stronger safeguards, civil penalties, and other relief.

The rise of autonomous AI attacks

The lawsuit comes amid growing concerns about increasingly capable AI models escaping controlled cybersecurity evaluations and attacking organizations outside their intended testing environments.

These autonomous attacks are not limited to OpenAI agents, with other AI platforms disclosing similar incidents in the past.

In July, Anthropic disclosed that its Claude models had breached production systems at three organizations during cybersecurity evaluations. One model created and uploaded a malicious Python package to the public PyPI repository, where it was downloaded and executed on 15 real systems.

This led Anthropic to remove internet access from all internal AI model evaluations following additional incidents involving unauthorized activity against government websites and other external systems.

Google also confirmed to The Wall Street Journal in September that its Gemini AI model had accessed the internet and hacked three companies during cybersecurity testing conducted in May.

California's lawsuit argues that OpenAI's failure to address these risks adequately has exposed organizations and the public to unnecessary cybersecurity threats, even as it told customers that its AI development practices were safe.

Title: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
Context: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical...
Full Text: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence. Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks. In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys. “Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models. In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks. “The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote. The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt. In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.” Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image. While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote. None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker. “The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.” The FBI weighs in The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.” The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants. After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October. However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI. The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert. These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

In this article

Attackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate cyberattacks, the FBI warns

Some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours

The attacks target organizations, potentially putting customers’ personal information at risk

Cybercriminals have found another AI tool to do more of the hacking for them.

The FBI issued a FLASH advisory on November 13 warning that attackers are abusing ARTEX, a tool originally developed for authorized security testing, to automate intrusions against organizations worldwide. In some observed attacks, criminals went from selecting a target to gaining privileged access in under three hours, leaving defenders little time to respond.

ARTEX is an open-source penetration-testing framework. Penetration testing means trying to break into systems with the owner’s permission to find weaknesses before criminals do.

An operator gives ARTEX a target and an objective. Its a planning agent divides the work into tasks, while other AI agents use security tools to carry them out and share their findings. Rather than having its own AI model, ARTEX connects to external large language models (LLMs). Once a task begins, it requires relatively little human input.

The FBI says attackers have used ARTEX since at least August against sectors including finance, government, healthcare, and technology. Separately, Microsoft reported that a China-state-aligned group used ARTEX to accelerate attacks after compromising ConnectWise application credentials.

While these attacks can generate plenty of suspicious activity, their speed leaves defenders little time to respond. An alert is only useful if defenders can investigate and act before the damage is done.

ARTEX helps attackers connect individual weaknesses into a bigger intrusion. An overlooked employee portal or exposed cloud credential can become a route to sensitive records, additional accounts, or connected organizations. For home users, that could mean personal information stolen from a company is later used for fraud or targeted scams.

How to stay safe

ARTEX changes how quickly attackers can work. It does not make basic security controls obsolete, but it makes leaving familiar weaknesses unfixed more dangerous. Most of the FBI’s recommendations are aimed at organizations. Businesses and IT teams should:

Stay up to date: Patch internet-facing systems promptly and inventory overlooked applications, including old employee and supplier portals. Restrict administrative interfaces to approved access paths.

Protect credentials and limit permissions: Scan for exposed passwords and API keys, rotate compromised secrets, and give applications only the access they need.

Monitor and log: Watch for rapid bursts of requests, unusual data access, and unexpected credential or privilege changes. Prepare procedures to revoke access and isolate affected systems quickly.

For individuals and small-business users, the fundamentals still matter:

Update your devices and software.

Use strong, unique passwords and turn on multi-factor authentication wherever available.

Run an up-to-date real-time anti-malware solution on your devices.

If a company tells you your account or information was affected, verify the notice through its official website or app and follow its incident-specific instructions.

Title: Retadup Worm Resurfaces 7 Years After Takedown to Spread CoffeeLoader Malware
Context: " CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new variant of CoffeeLoader, a malware designed to deliver additional payloads to infected machines.

"On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named '7z.dll' into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe," Kaspersky said in an analysis published today.

"The '7z.dll' file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer."

CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode. The malware is assessed to share source code similarities with another loader family tracked as SmokeLoader.

Malware packed with Armory uses file names like "ArmouryAIOSDK.dll" and "ArmouryA.dll," with the packer hijacking some of the original Armoury Crate functionality with self-decrypting shellcode.

Notably, the shellcode extracts code that executes a decryption routine on a system's GPU by making use of the OpenCL library. The end goal is to install CoffeeLoader, establish persistence, and execute it by injecting it into a newly created "dllhost.exe" process.

The latest version of the packer continues to use the GPU, but replaces OpenCL with the OpenGL library. In addition, the new version of the packer delivers intermediate shellcode instead of a DLL. This shellcode serves as a downloader responsible for fetching the main CoffeeLoader malware.

"To establish persistence, the Trojan copies '7z.dll' to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%," Kaspersky said. "The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information."

"To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager."

Once persistence is successful, the malware launches one of the legitimate processes (e.g., "dllhost.exe," "WerFault.exe," "svchost.exe," "OpenWith.exe," or "AtBroker.exe") and then injects itself into it, after which the malware shellcode is downloaded from a hard-coded command-and-control (C2) server.

The shellcode then decrypts and runs the CoffeeLoader payload. It supports the same three commands to run the next-stage malware from the C2 server -

Injecting it into a process

Saving it to disk as an executable and then running it

Saving it as a DLL and then running it via "rundll32.exe"

As for how CoffeeLoader is distributed, it takes place via Retadup, a Windows computer worm that was disrupted by French law enforcement authorities in August 2019. The malware, which spreads via infected USB drives, has been used to drop additional payloads like cryptocurrency miners, the Stop ransomware, and the Arkei password stealer.

"Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware," Kaspersky said. "At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader."

It remains unclear whether the worm's author or some other threat actor was instrumental in bringing the C2 servers back online. Kaspersky said it blocked around 15,000 systems from being infected with the resurrected version of the worm, most of them located in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

Title: FBI Highlights Growing Abuse of AI-Driven Pentesting Framework ARTEX
Context: Read more about ARTEX: India Warns of New AI-Driven Cyber-Attacks Targeting Financial and Crypto Businesses ARTEX Origins and LLM Integration ARTEX is an open-source, AI model-...
Full Text:
The FBI has warned of a growing number of malicious cyber intrusion campaigns leveraging the open-source, AI-powered penetration testing tool ARTEX.

In a FBI Flash notice, published on November 13, the Bureau said a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally since at least August 2026.

Targets range across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal industries.

Recent incidents have included financially motivated attacks against South Korean financial institutions which resulted in the exfiltration of personal information from approximately 67,000 individuals and a supply chain compromise affecting ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers that enabled access to more than 2250 downstream tenants.

The FBI noted that ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques and some intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.

Read more about ARTEX: India Warns of New AI-Driven Cyber-Attacks Targeting Financial and Crypto Businesses

ARTEX Origins and LLM Integration

ARTEX is an open-source, AI model-driven, autonomous penetration testing framework released on GitHub by a user known as ‘Autumn-27’ in July 2026.

Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs).

The FBI highlighted that ARTEX does not include its own AI model, rather it integrates with external LLM providers, including frontier models (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT) and open-source or Chinese-origin models (DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, Kimi).

“Analysis of attacker-controlled ARTEX instances shows Chinese models are most prevalent, with DeepSeek Flash family models dominating usage due to their balance of capabilities, relatively low cost and lack of observable guardrails when framed for penetration testing,” the FBI notice read.

The original GitHub repository for ARTEX was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse. The author claimed they were not involved in the ARTEX-linked attacks and that the tool was only meant for authorized penetration testing.

Nevertheless, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO.

Key Risks: Automation, Overlooked Systems and Supply Chain Attacks

The FBI assessed that ARTEX poses several risks as threat actors adopt it.

It automates the time-consuming enumeration and exploitation phases of intrusions, allowing even small groups to run multiple campaigns at once.

It also lowers the technical barrier to entry, enabling actors with minimal expertise to carry out sophisticated attacks.

ARTEX is particularly effective at finding and exploiting overlooked systems that receive less security attention than flagship applications, such as partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee and sales-support tools, legacy services and third-party integrations.

It has also demonstrated supply chain capabilities, including modifying iOS application distribution infrastructure through exposed cloud credentials. By mapping trust relationships between organizations, it can compromise weaker vendors or CI/CD pipelines and pivot into high-value enterprise networks.

Although ARTEX generates noisy traffic that may trigger alerts, its speed leaves defenders little time to coordinate a response before attackers achieve their objectives.

The FBI provided a list of recommended security controls and operational measures organizations can take to prevent and mitigate ARTEX.

The Bureau is also seeking any helpful information on ARTEX and malicious campaigns using the tool, including infrastructure artifacts, authentication and access logs, application and API activity, LLM and AI infrastructure indicators, cloud and container activity and exploitation and persistence artifacts.

Title: Information Commissioner’s Office Receives 300+ Reports of Medical Snooping
Context: In May, 11 staff were sacked and 14 given written warnings after unlawfully accessing the records of victims of the 2023 Nottingham knife attacks
Full Text:
The UK’s data protection watchdog has written to health service leaders after receiving hundreds of reports of staff illegally accessing patient records.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) said it has asked over 200 NHS bosses across the UK to provide personal assurances that measures are in place to prevent and detect unauthorized insider access.

The letter itself details four areas that healthcare organizations must focus on: effective access controls, effective auditing and monitoring for unauthorized access, regular training for staff and consistent action when things go wrong.

“You should investigate suspected unauthorized access promptly and consistently. You should consider the impact on the person affected, including your obligations to notify the individual,” it said. “You should also consider your obligations to notify the ICO. Where you establish wrongdoing, you should take appropriate disciplinary, professional, regulatory or other action.”

The ICO said it has already received over 300 reports of unauthorized access by NHS staff, including workers looking at records with no legitimate need, and viewing or sharing the records of people they know.

Read more on NHS data leaks: ICO Cautions Healthcare Worker After Princess of Wales Incident

The letter comes on the back of several high-profile incidents impacting the health service.

In May, 11 staff were sacked and 14 given written warnings after unlawfully accessing the records of victims of the 2023 Nottingham knife attacks. A month later a Cambridgeshire hospital launched an investigation after around 40 staff accessed the records of a seriously injured child without good reason.

In June the ICO issued a former healthcare worker a formal caution after they tried to access and sell the medical records of the Princess of Wales at a private hospital.

What the ICO Wants to Know

ICO chief executive, Paul Arnold, sent out practical advice and recommendations to healthcare organizations back in June.

In his new letter, he said that NHS chief executives need the right processes, culture and behaviors in place to safeguard patient data.

“Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardise the vital trust people place in our health service,” Arnold added.

“This message goes beyond the health sector: any organization entrusted with people's most sensitive information has a duty to protect it and we will take action if they fall short. I strongly encourage leaders in every sector to ask themselves whether their safeguards would stand up to the same scrutiny.”

The ICO is now asking NHS CEOs to confirm that their organization is:

Actively and continuously managing access to patient records

Spotting suspicious access using effective monitoring and audit systems

Confident that every member of staff knows what is expected of them what the consequences are of illegally accessing medical records

Investigating suspected unauthorized access promptly and taking appropriate action if wrongdoing is established

“Senior leaders should confirm that they have reviewed their organization’s approach in these areas within the past six months,” the ICO said. “Those who have not are expected to complete a review within the next three months. The responses will help shape the regulator’s next steps to respond to this issue and help protect patient’s privacy.”

Title: Italy Fines Meta €805 Million Over Facebook's Android Gallery Access Without Explicit Consent
Context: The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata...
Full Text:
Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for them to post.

The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent.

The company has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately.

Meta plans to appeal and calls the fine "disproportionate", a spokesperson said in a statement reported by Reuters.

The app asks for gallery access via a single permission that covers the whole app and several functions with different purposes, the authority found. A general notice about enabling other features appears first, but it does not make it clear to users that they are also enabling gallery suggestions.

Fully granted, a permission like this lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive, usually on an ongoing basis. Neither the user nor the authority can check which information is actually used.

The authority found a breach of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which puts the EU's ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats a phone as part of a person's private life. Any access to what the phone stores, therefore, requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results.

The authority's order, set out in its press release, requires the company to:

Within 60 days, ask for consent through a separate, specific request for this feature, and explain clearly what the feature is for, that it accesses the gallery, and how to turn it off.

Within 60 days, keep the feature off by default, including for people who already granted the permission.

Within 30 days, report to the authority on the work it has started, and within 90 days, on the measures it has taken.

If the company misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent.

Meta said in a statement quoted in a Reuters report that the feature works only after users give permission on their device, and that they can change that permission at any time in their settings.

The Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti, the Bolzano consumer protection group whose complaint started the investigation, published consumer advice on July 11, 2025. It told users to switch off the gallery suggestion settings in the app and to check what access and permissions the Facebook app has on their phone.

The investigation did not look at whether gallery content was used to train AI models. The company denies any such use. The authority may separately examine a newer feature, launched this year, that allows gallery content to be processed in the cloud.

The company had argued that Ireland's data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules do not provide a one-stop-shop mechanism.

The feature has been available since 2023. The investigation began in July 2025 and included the authority's own technical analysis.

The fine equals about 0.47% of the group's global revenue. In setting it, the authority weighed the large number of people involved, about 20 million Android users in Italy.

It also weighed how long the breach has lasted. The breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the app, and for those who have already granted permission, the authority said.

Other factors were a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation. Changes the company made after the complaint counted in its favor, though the authority judged them late and limited to people who update the app.
